claim: MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells were phenotypically sorted into highly migratory (MDA+) and weakly migratory (MDA-) subpopulations through 20 rounds of transwell migration assays.
source: Twenty rounds of sorting resulted in the isolation of two stable subpopulations of breast cancer cells: highly migratory MDA+ and weakly migratory MDA- (Figure 1a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure and Figure 1a shows the schematic of phenotypic sorting.

claim: Highly migratory MDA+ and weakly migratory MDA- subpopulations formed orthotopic primary tumors that grew at comparable rates.
source: Consistent with our previous in vivo findings (Hapach et al., 2021), the highly migratory MDA+ subpopulation and the weakly migratory MDA- subpopulation formed orthotopic primary tumors that grew at comparable rates (Figure 1b–c)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b-c and cites previous work (Hapach et al., 2021).

claim: The MDA+ subpopulation was weakly metastatic while the MDA- subpopulation was highly metastatic in vivo.
source: the MDA+ subpopulation was weakly metastatic while the MDA- subpopulation was highly metastatic in vivo (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by BLI imaging data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: MDA- primary tumors exhibited significantly higher tumor stiffness compared to MDA+ tumors.
source: Based on atomic force microscopy measurements, MDA- primary tumors exhibited significantly higher tumor stiffness compared to MDA+ tumors (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM measurements shown in Figure 1e.

claim: MDA- tumors had significantly higher amounts of mouse-derived matrix components including collagen I, fibronectin 1, collagen IV, tenascin-C, and periostin compared to MDA+ tumors.
source: qPCR of tumors revealed significantly higher amounts of mouse-derived matrix, including collagen I (Col1a1), fibronectin 1 (Fn1), collagen IV (Col4a1), tenascin-C (Tnc), and periostin (Postn), in MDA- tumors compared to MDA+ tumors (Figure 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Increased collagen and fibronectin was evident in MDA- tumors compared to MDA+ tumors via immunohistochemical staining.
source: Similarly, increased collagen and fibronectin was evident via immunohistochemical staining in MDA- tumors compared to MDA+ tumors (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Weakly migratory, highly metastatic MDA- cells form stiffer tumors with increased ECM compared to highly migratory, weakly metastatic MDA+ cells.
source: These results indicate that the weakly migratory, highly metastatic MDA- form stiffer tumors with increased ECM compared to the highly migratory, weakly metastatic MDA+.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the AFM and matrix component data presented earlier.

claim: MDA- tumors exhibited increased levels of several CAF markers including α-smooth muscle actin, fibroblast activation protein, and platelet-derived growth factor receptors α and β.
source: MDA- tumors exhibited increased levels of several CAF markers, including α-smooth muscle actin (Acta2), fibroblast activation protein (Fap), and platelet-derived growth factor receptors α and β (Pdgfra, Pdgfrb) (Figure 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA expression data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: MDA- tumors exhibited an increased fraction of αSMA positive tissue area compared to MDA+ tumors.
source: MDA- tumors also exhibited an increased fraction of αSMA positive tissue area compared to MDA+ tumors (Figure 1i-j).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 1i-j.

claim: MDA- tumors are enriched for a myCAF-like fibroblast population.
source: Given that αSMA is the primary marker of myofibroblast-like CAFs (myCAFs), that myCAFs and matrix-CAFs (mCAFs) express high levels of Fap, Pdgfra, and Pdgfrb (Öhlund et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2020; Bartoschek et al., 2018), and that myCAFs are highly contractile and deposit high levels of ECM (Wu et al., 2020; Kieffer et al., 2020), these results suggest that MDA- tumors are enriched for a myCAF-like fibroblast population.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the CAF marker data and supported by citations to literature on myCAF characteristics.

claim: Weakly migratory, highly metastatic MDA- primary tumors have increased myCAF-like fibroblasts.
source: These findings reveal that the weakly migratory, highly metastatic MDA- primary tumors have increased myCAF-like fibroblasts.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the CAF marker and αSMA data presented earlier.

claim: No significant difference in Stroma-Activating Score was calculated between MDA+ and MDA-.
source: No significant difference in Stroma-Activating Score was calculated between MDA+ and MDA- (Figure 1l).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1l.

claim: MDA+ scored significantly higher on Matrix Ligands, while MDA- scored significantly higher on Cell-Cell Adhesion and Secreted genes.
source: However, when separated into several Stroma-Activating Groups (Inflammatory, Matrix Ligands, Cell-Cell Adhesion, and Secreted), MDA+ scored significantly higher on Matrix Ligands, while MDA- scored significantly higher on Cell-Cell Adhesion and Secreted genes (Figure 1m–p).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1m-p.

claim: Both TGFB2 and TGM2 were significantly enriched in MDA- compared to MDA+.
source: Both TGFB2 and TGM2 were significantly enriched in MDA- compared to MDA+.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data on secreted factors involved in fibroblast activation.

claim: MDA- activate fibroblasts through secreted factors.
source: These findings suggest that MDA- activate fibroblasts through secreted factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data showing enrichment of secreted genes in MDA-.

claim: MDA- released significantly more MVs than MDA+.
source: MDA- released significantly more MVs than MDA+ (Figure 2a)
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoparticle tracking analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Both MV+ and MV- had similar size distributions and were within the expected 200 nm – 1 µm range.
source: but both MV+ and MV- had similar size distributions and were within the expected 200 nm – 1 µm range (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by size distribution data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: MV- caused focal adhesion kinase (FAK) Tyr397 phosphorylation in fibroblasts.
source: MV- caused focal adhesion kinase (FAK) Tyr397 phosphorylation in fibroblasts, as increased FAK phosphorylation (pFAK) was evident in fibroblasts cultured with MV- compared to control and MV+ conditions (Figure 2d–e)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2d-e.

claim: MDA-MB-231 MVs regulate fibroblast FAK activation.
source: consistent with previous findings that MDA-MB-231 MVs regulate fibroblast FAK activation (Antonyak et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim cites previous work by Antonyak et al., 2011.

claim: Fibroblasts cultured with MV- exhibited increased α-smooth muscle actin (αSMA) expression and cell area compared to both control and MV+ conditions.
source: Additionally, fibroblasts cultured with MV- exhibited increased α-smooth muscle actin (αSMA) expression, a marker of fibroblast activation, and cell area compared to both control and MV+ conditions (Figure 2f–h, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and microscopy data shown in Figure 2f-h and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Fibroblasts cultured with MV+ displayed no change in αSMA expression or cell area compared to control conditions.
source: Fibroblasts cultured with MV+ displayed no change in αSMA expression or cell area compared to control conditions (Figure 2f–h, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and microscopy data shown in Figure 2f-h and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Fibroblasts cultured with MV- displayed increased positive fibronectin staining, suggesting MV- increased fibronectin deposition by fibroblasts.
source: Fibroblasts cultured with MV- also displayed increased positive fibronectin staining (Figure 2i, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–c), suggesting the MV- increased fibronectin deposition by fibroblasts.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2i and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b-c.

claim: Fibroblasts cultured with MV- exhibited increased EdU incorporation compared to MV+ and control conditions, indicative of increased proliferation.
source: Fibroblasts cultured with MV- exhibited increased EdU incorporation compared to MV+ and control conditions, indicative of increased proliferation (Figure 2j, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 2j and Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Increased traction force and traction stress was evident in fibroblasts cultured with MV-, compared to control conditions, but not in fibroblasts cultured with MV+.
source: Increased traction force and traction stress was evident in fibroblasts cultured with MV-, compared to control conditions, but not in fibroblasts cultured with MV+ (Figure 2k, Figure 2—figure supplement 1e–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by traction force microscopy data shown in Figure 2k and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e-f.

claim: MV- activate fibroblasts to a more proliferative, contractile state compared to MV+ and control conditions.
source: Overall, this data indicates that MV- activate fibroblasts to a more proliferative, contractile state compared to MV+ and control conditions.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the fibroblast phenotype data presented earlier.

claim: MDA- spheroids exhibited minimal spheroid outgrowth after 48 hr of culture.
source: After 48 hr of culture, MDA- spheroids exhibited minimal spheroid outgrowth, measured using a spheroid area index (A48h/A0h-1) (Figure 2l–m, Figure 2—figure supplement 1g–h)
evidence: The claim is supported by spheroid outgrowth data shown in Figure 2l-m and Figure 2—figure supplement 1g-h.

claim: MDA+ spheroids exhibited high levels of spheroid outgrowth.
source: while MDA+ spheroids exhibited high levels of spheroid outgrowth (Figure 2o–p, Figure 2—figure supplement 1g and j), consistent with our previous findings (Hapach et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by spheroid outgrowth data shown in Figure 2o-p and Figure 2—figure supplement 1g and j, and cites previous work.

claim: Coculture of MDA- or MDA+ with 3T3 fibroblasts resulted in significantly enhanced spheroid outgrowth compared to cancer cells alone.
source: Coculture of MDA- or MDA+ with 3T3 fibroblasts (MDA-+3 T3, MDA++3 T3) resulted in significantly enhanced spheroid outgrowth compared to cancer cells alone (Figure 2l–m and o–p, Figure 2—figure supplement 1g–h and j).
evidence: The claim is supported by spheroid coculture data shown in Figure 2l-m and o-p, Figure 2—figure supplement 1g-h and j.

claim: MDA-+3T3 spheroids displayed fibroblast-led strands of MDA- migration away from the spheroid, suggesting that fibroblasts physically lead the migration of MDA- through the matrix.
source: MDA-+3 T3 spheroids displayed fibroblast-led strands of MDA- migration away from the spheroid, suggesting that the fibroblasts physically lead the migration of MDA- through the matrix (Figure 2n).
evidence: The claim is supported by time series imaging shown in Figure 2n.

claim: MDA-+3T3 spheroids cultured with MV- exhibited significantly enhanced spheroid outgrowth and MDA- migration distance, compared to MDA-+3T3 control spheroids.
source: Importantly, MDA-+3 T3 spheroids cultured with MV- exhibited significantly enhanced spheroid outgrowth and MDA- migration distance, compared to MDA-+3 T3 control spheroids (Figure 2l–m, Figure 2—figure supplement 1g–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by spheroid outgrowth data shown in Figure 2l-m and Figure 2—figure supplement 1g-h.

claim: MDA-+3T3 spheroids cultured with MV+ showed increased outgrowth compared to MDA-+3T3 spheroids, but this outgrowth was significantly less than that induced by MV-.
source: MDA-+3 T3 spheroids cultured with MV+ also showed increased outgrowth compared to MDA-+3 T3 spheroids, but this outgrowth was significantly less than that induced by MV- (Figure 2l–m, Figure 2—figure supplement 1g–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by spheroid outgrowth data shown in Figure 2l-m and Figure 2—figure supplement 1g-h.

claim: MDA++3T3 spheroids cultured with MV+ or MV- exhibited no change in spheroid outgrowth and MDA+ migration distance compared to control conditions.
source: Interestingly, MDA++3 T3 spheroids cultured with MV+ or MV- exhibited no change in spheroid outgrowth and MDA+ migration distance compared to control conditions (Figure 2o–p, Figure 2—figure supplement 1g and j).
evidence: The claim is supported by spheroid outgrowth data shown in Figure 2o-p and Figure 2—figure supplement 1g and j.

claim: MDA+ are capable of robust migration independently of MV-mediated fibroblast signaling.
source: This result suggests that MDA+ are capable of robust migration independently of MV-mediated fibroblast signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that MDA+ spheroid outgrowth is not affected by MVs.

claim: When MV- were applied to MDA- only spheroids, no increase in spheroid outgrowth was observed, highlighting the necessity of fibroblasts for MV-induced cancer cell migration.
source: When MV- were applied to MDA- only spheroids, no increase in spheroid outgrowth was observed, highlighting the necessity of fibroblasts for this MV-induced cancer cell migration (Figure 2l–m, Figure 2—figure supplement 1g–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by spheroid outgrowth data shown in Figure 2l-m and Figure 2—figure supplement 1g-h.

claim: MDA- spheroids cultured with fibroblast conditioned media or MV--treated fibroblast conditioned media displayed no change in spheroid outgrowth.
source: Additionally, MDA- spheroids cultured with fibroblast conditioned media or MV--treated fibroblast conditioned media displayed no change in spheroid outgrowth (Figure 2—figure supplement 1i)
evidence: The claim is supported by spheroid outgrowth data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Fibroblast-enhanced cancer cell migration is not a result of secreted factors but rather due to physical interactions.
source: indicating that fibroblast-enhanced cancer cell migration is not a result of secreted factors but rather due to physical interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conditioned media experiment results.

claim: MV- are potent activators of fibroblasts and MV--induced fibroblast activation mechanically feeds back to induce the migration of MDA-.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that MV- are potent activators of fibroblasts and that MV--induced fibroblast activation mechanically feeds back to induce the migration of MDA-.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the fibroblast activation and spheroid migration data presented earlier.

claim: MV cargo was different between highly migratory and weakly migratory subpopulations of breast cancer cells, with 26.8% of identified proteins being more highly expressed by MV+ and 29.8% being more highly expressed by MV-.
source: Proteomics data suggests that MV cargo was different between highly migratory and weakly migratory subpopulations of breast cancer cells, with 26.8% of the identified proteins being more highly expressed by MV+ (FC ≥1.1) and 29.8% being more highly expressed by MV- (FC ≤0.9) (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by iTRAQ proteomics data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: 43.4% of identified proteins were similarly expressed between both MV populations.
source: 43.4% of identified proteins were similarly expressed between both MV populations (0.9<FC < 1.1) (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by iTRAQ proteomics data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: MV+ were enriched for cargo involved in biological adhesion, cell adhesion, location, and cell motility.
source: Of note, MV+ were enriched for cargo involved in biological adhesion, cell adhesion, location, and cell motility (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by PSEA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: MV- were enriched for cargo involved in various metabolic and catabolic processes and vesicle-mediated transport.
source: MV- were enriched for cargo involved in various metabolic and catabolic processes and vesicle-mediated transport (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by PSEA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Cancer cells with varying migratory ability release MVs with distinctly different cargo.
source: These findings indicate that cancer cells with varying migratory ability release MVs with distinctly different cargo.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the proteomics data presented earlier.

claim: 79% of genes/proteins identified in both RNA-seq and proteomics datasets were expressed at similar levels between cells and MVs.
source: 79% of genes/proteins identified in both datasets (1786 of 2260) were expressed at similar levels between cells and MVs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNA-seq and proteomics data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The majority of genes/proteins identified by RNA-seq and proteomics are expressed at similar levels between the MDA subpopulations and their respective MVs, reinforcing the notion that MVs reflect the composition of the MV-releasing cell.
source: These results highlight that the majority of genes/proteins identified by RNA-seq and proteomics are expressed at similar levels between the MDA subpopulations and their respective MVs, reinforcing the notion that MVs reflect the composition of the MV-releasing cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of RNA-seq and proteomics data.

claim: MV- had significantly higher expression of TGM2 compared to MV+.
source: MV- had significantly higher expression of TGM2 compared to MV+, while TGFB1, TGFB2, NOTCH2, and S100A11 had no significant difference in expression between MV+ and MV- (Figure 3b and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 3b and d.

claim: TIMP3, FN1, and COL8A1 matrix-remodeling proteins were expressed significantly higher in MV+ while PLOD3, TGM2, COL12A1, and PLOD1 were expressed significantly higher in MV-.
source: TIMP3, FN1, and COL8A1 matrix-remodeling proteins were expressed significantly higher in MV+ while PLOD3, TGM2, COL12A1, and PLOD1 were expressed significantly higher in MV- (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: Tissue transglutaminase 2 (Tg2) is a calcium-dependent enzyme that both crosslinks collagen and activates fibroblasts.
source: Tissue transglutaminase 2, also known as TGM2 or Tg2, identified as significantly enriched in MV- compared to MV+, is a calcium-dependent enzyme that both crosslinks collagen and activates fibroblasts (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Tg2 function.

claim: EVs have previously been shown to transfer Tg2 to fibroblasts resulting in fibroblast activation.
source: EVs have previously been shown to transfer Tg2 to fibroblasts resulting in fibroblast activation (Antonyak et al., 2011; Shinde et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites previous work by Antonyak et al., 2011 and Shinde et al., 2020.

claim: Increased Tg2 expression in MDA- and MV-, compared to MDA+ and MV+, was verified using western blot.
source: Increased Tg2 expression in MDA- and MV-, compared to MDA+ and MV+, was verified using western blot (Figure 3e–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3e-h.

claim: EV-Tg2 crosslinks EV-fibronectin (Fn) into dimers to potentiate fibroblast integrin signaling upon EV-fibroblast interactions.
source: It has also been shown that EV-Tg2 crosslinks EV-fibronectin (Fn) into dimers to potentiate fibroblast integrin signaling upon EV-fibroblast interactions (Antonyak et al., 2011; Shinde et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites previous work by Antonyak et al., 2011 and Shinde et al., 2020.

claim: The Fn dimer was present in both MV+ and MV-, but was more highly expressed in MV+.
source: While the Fn dimer was present in both MV+ and MV-, it was more highly expressed in MV+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Fibroblast activation by MV- does not solely rely on Fn dimer-mediated integrin signaling.
source: suggesting that fibroblast activation by MV- does not solely rely on Fn dimer-mediated integrin signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that MV+ have more Fn dimer but less fibroblast activation capacity.

claim: Knockdown of Tg2 resulted in no change in MDA- migration or MV release compared to the scrambled control.
source: Knockdown of Tg2 resulted in no change in MDA- migration or MV release compared to the scrambled control (MDA- (scr)) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by migration and MV release data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c-d.

claim: A slight decrease in transwell invasion was observed in MDA- (shTg2) compared to MDA- (scr).
source: A slight decrease in transwell invasion was observed in MDA- (shTg2) compared to MDA- (scr) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell invasion data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: MVs released from MDA- (shTg2) had reduced Tg2 expression compared to the scrambled control MVs.
source: MVs released from MDA- (shTg2) (MV- (shTg2)) had reduced Tg2 expression compared to the scrambled control MVs (MV- (scr)) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f-g.

claim: 50.05% of proteins identified using proteomics were detected at similar levels between MV- (scr) and MV- (shTg2), 25.5% of proteins were enriched in MV- (scr), and 24.45% of proteins were enriched in MV- (shTg2).
source: 50.05% of proteins identified using proteomics were detected at similar levels between MV- (scr) and MV- (shTg2), 25.5% of proteins were enriched in MV- (scr), and 24.45% of proteins were enriched in MV- (shTg2) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Knockdown of Tg2 affected a variety of cell processes and resulted in different MV protein expression.
source: These findings indicate that knockdown of Tg2 affected a variety of cell processes and resulted in different MV protein expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PSEA analysis of MV- (scr) and MV- (shTg2).

claim: Tg2 was significantly enriched in MV- (scr) compared to MV- (shTg2).
source: As expected, Tg2 was significantly enriched in MV- (scr) compared to MV- (shTg2) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1k).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1k.

claim: S100A11 was significantly enriched in MV- (scr) compared to MV- (shTg2).
source: S100A11 was also significantly enriched in MV- (scr) compared to MV- (shTg2) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1k).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1k.

claim: S100A11 released by cancer cells is known to stimulate a change in fibroblast phenotype upon binding to the RAGE receptor.
source: Importantly, S100A11 released by cancer cells is known to stimulate a change in fibroblast phenotype upon binding to the RAGE receptor (Mitsui et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim cites previous work by Mitsui et al., 2019.

claim: Dimerization of S100A11 by Tg2 is required for S100A11-RAGE binding.
source: Dimerization of S100A11 by Tg2 is required for S100A11-RAGE binding (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites previous work by Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: Any effects on fibroblast activation due to an upregulation of MV S100A11 is likely due to Tg2 signaling.
source: Therefore, any effects on fibroblast activation due to an upregulation of MV S100A11 is likely due to Tg2 signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement of Tg2 for S100A11-RAGE binding.

claim: All other fibroblast-activating and matrix-remodeling proteins in MVs identified with proteomics were not significantly altered by Tg2 knockdown.
source: All other fibroblast-activating and matrix-remodeling proteins in MVs identified with proteomics were not significant altered by Tg2 knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 1k).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1k.

claim: Fibroblasts cultured with MV- (shTg2) exhibited decreased αSMA expression, cell area, fibronectin area, proliferation, and traction force, compared to culture with MV- (scr).
source: Fibroblasts cultured with MV- (shTg2) exhibited decreased αSMA expression, cell area, fibronectin area, proliferation, and traction force, compared to culture with MV- (scr) (Figure 4a–f, Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple assays shown in Figure 4a-f and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a-g.

claim: Knockdown of Tg2 in MDA- cells reduced the capacity of MV- to activate fibroblasts.
source: This suggests that knockdown of Tg2 in MDA- cells reduced the capacity of MV- to activate fibroblasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced fibroblast activation phenotypes observed with MV- (shTg2).

claim: Treatment of MV- with the Tg2 inhibitor, T101, decreased fibroblast αSMA expression compared to culture with MV-.
source: Treatment of MV- with the Tg2 inhibitor, T101, decreased fibroblast αSMA expression compared to culture with MV-, further supporting role of MV-Tg2 in fibroblast activation (Figure 4h–i).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4h-i.

claim: MDA- (shTg2) + 3T3 spheroids cultured with MV- (shTg2) exhibited no change in spheroid outgrowth compared to untreated control conditions.
source: MDA- (shTg2) + 3 T3 spheroids cultured with MV- (shTg2) exhibited no change in spheroid outgrowth compared to untreated control conditions (Figure 4j–k, Figure 4—figure supplement 2g)
evidence: The claim is supported by spheroid outgrowth data shown in Figure 4j-k and Figure 4—figure supplement 2g.

claim: Without Tg2, fibroblasts could not increase cancer cell migration.
source: suggesting that without Tg2, fibroblasts could not increase cancer cell migration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spheroid outgrowth data with Tg2 knockdown.

claim: MDA- (shTg2) +3T3 spheroids cultured with MV- (scr) exhibited a significant increase in spheroid migration compared to untreated conditions, highlighting that MV-Tg2 is required for MV-mediated fibroblast-induced cancer cell migration.
source: MDA- (shTg2) +3 T3 spheroids cultured with MV- (scr) exhibited a significant increase in spheroid migration compared to untreated conditions, highlighting that MV-Tg2 is required for MV-mediated fibroblast-induced cancer cell migration (Figure 4j–k, Figure 4—figure supplement 2g).
evidence: The claim is supported by spheroid outgrowth data shown in Figure 4j-k and Figure 4—figure supplement 2g.

claim: Fibroblasts cultured with MV+ (FUW-Tg2) displayed increased cell area and increased traction force, compared to culture with MV+.
source: Fibroblasts cultured with MV+ (FUW-Tg2) displayed increased cell area and increased traction force, compared to culture with MV+ (Figure 4—figure supplement 3b–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell area and traction force data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3b-c.

claim: MV-Tg2 regulates MV-mediated fibroblast phenotype.
source: These results were consistent with earlier findings suggesting that MV-Tg2 regulates MV-mediated fibroblast phenotype (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the Tg2 overexpression data.

claim: Overexpression of Tg2 did not significantly change the motile fraction of MCF7 in 3D collagen gels.
source: Overexpression of Tg2 did not significantly change the motile fraction of MCF7 in 3D collagen gels (Figure 4—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3e.

claim: Fibroblasts cultured with MVMCF7 (FUW-Tg2) displayed significantly increased cell area compared to control or +MVMCF7 conditions and exhibited significantly increased traction force compared to control conditions.
source: Fibroblasts cultured with MVMCF7 (FUW-Tg2) displayed significantly increased cell area compared to control or +MVMCF7 conditions and exhibited significantly increased traction force compared to control conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell area and traction force data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3f-g.

claim: Addition of Tg2 to MVs from a weakly migratory breast cancer cell line regulates MV-mediated fibroblast phenotype.
source: These findings confirm that addition of Tg2 to MVs from a weakly migratory breast cancer cell line regulates MV-mediated fibroblast phenotype.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the MCF7 Tg2 overexpression data.

claim: MCF7 +3T3 spheroids cultured with MVMCF7 (FUW-Tg2) exhibited significantly higher levels of spheroid outgrowth and MCF7 cells migrating away from the spheroid core were observed.
source: MCF7 +3 T3 spheroids cultured with MVMCF7 (FUW-Tg2) exhibited significantly higher levels of spheroid outgrowth and MCF7 cells migrating away from the spheroid core were observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 3h–i, red arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by spheroid outgrowth data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3h-i.

claim: MV-mediated fibroblast activation induced by Tg2 overexpression can enhance the dissemination of the MCF7 weakly migratory breast cancer cell line.
source: These results reveal that MV-mediated fibroblast activation induced by Tg2 overexpression can enhance the dissemination of the MCF7 weakly migratory breast cancer cell line.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the MCF7 spheroid outgrowth data with Tg2 overexpression.

claim: Purified Tg2 (1 µg/mL) significantly increased fibroblast cell area and fibroblast traction force compared to control conditions.
source: Purified Tg2 (1 µg/mL) significantly increased fibroblast cell area and fibroblast traction force compared to control conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3j–k).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell area and traction force data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3j-k.

claim: The increased fibroblast area and traction force induced by purified Tg2 were comparable to levels induced by MV-.
source: The increased fibroblast area and traction force induced by purified Tg2 were comparable to levels induced by MV- (Figure 4—figure supplement 3j–k).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of purified Tg2 and MV- effects shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3j-k.

claim: Tg2 alone can induce a change in fibroblast phenotype and Tg2 packaging by MVs is not essential for Tg2-mediated fibroblast activation.
source: These results reveal that Tg2 alone can induce a change in fibroblast phenotype and that Tg2 packaging by MVs is not essential for Tg2-mediated fibroblast activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the purified Tg2 experiment results.

claim: Six weeks post subcutaneous injection of MDA- (scr) and MDA- (shTg2) into the mammary fat pad, primary tumors were of similar volumes.
source: Six weeks post subcutaneous injection of MDA- (scr) and MDA- (shTg2) into the mammary fat pad, primary tumors were of similar volumes (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor volume data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: MDA- (shTg2) tumors exhibited decreased stiffness compared to control tumors.
source: MDA- (shTg2) tumors exhibited decreased stiffness compared to control tumors (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM stiffness measurements shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Immunofluorescent staining of MDA- (scr) and MDA- (shTg2) tumors for αSMA revealed a decreased fraction of αSMA+ tissue in MDA- (shTg2) tumors compared to control tumors.
source: Immunofluorescent staining of MDA- (scr) and MDA- (shTg2) tumors for the fibroblast activation marker αSMA revealed a decreased fraction of αSMA+ tissue in MDA- (shTg2) tumors compared to control tumors (Figure 5d–e)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5d-e.

claim: Knockdown of Tg2 reduced primary tumor fibroblast activation.
source: suggesting that knockdown of Tg2 reduced primary tumor fibroblast activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the decreased αSMA+ tissue in MDA- (shTg2) tumors.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining for collagen and fibronectin revealed decreased matrix in the MDA- (shTg2) tumors compared to control tumors.
source: Immunohistochemical staining for collagen and fibronectin also revealed decreased matrix in the MDA- (shTg2) tumors compared to control tumors (Figure 5f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The metastasis of MDA-(shTg2) to the lungs and liver was greatly reduced compared to MDA- (scr).
source: The metastasis of MDA-(shTg2) to the lungs and liver was greatly reduced compared to MDA- (scr) (Figure 5g–k).
evidence: The claim is supported by BLI imaging and immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 5g-k.
